newsitem.title: UK: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - AXA/UAP IN BRITAIN.
newsitem.headline: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - AXA/UAP IN BRITAIN.

text.p: THE PROTEUS COLUMN

France's Axa has opted for the straightforward solution of a merger to solve the problem of its British inheritance from last year's merger with UAP. Axa owned Axa Equity & Law, while UAP owned the larger competitor Sun Life. When Axa merged with UAP, a decision about the British operations had to made.

There was initial talk of management buyouts or of one or other unit being sold. The obvious route of merging the two was complicated by the threat of large costs - Axa E&L had spent a lot of money on new property and technology - as well as job redundancies against stiff trade union opposition, and a potentially confused brand name.

The reason to merge anyway may be the prospect, however close, of a single European currency. Axa Equity & Law chief Mark Wood, the real driving force in the merger, is known to believe that after monetary union the ability to operate on a pan European or even global scale will be crucial to UK life insurers.

Reflecting views already common in the non-life sector, Wood doubts whether many UK firms could afford to make the investment necessary in production, distribution and branding, to guarantee long term success.

Quite how his newly merged group will get over its own branding hurdle is not clear. It combines not only Sun Life and Axa E&L, but also Provincial Insurance, a UAP subsidiary based in England's Lake District, which also has a direct operation called Prospero, and Axa's general insurance operation in Cardiff.
The indication from the rest of the merged Axa-UAP is that the Axa name will predominate in all operations in all countries. A considerable amount of money has been earmarked to ensure that effect.

But Sun Life is the bigger UK partner and the better known name. The UK insurance magazine Post reports Wood saying the company was "deep in research" on achieving a branding breakthrough. The market awaits the outcome.
If Wood's perception of the future is right, and he has a good track record, then consolidation in the life sector may accelerate.
Particularly in view of increasing demutualisation, return on capital may become the most significant driver of stock values. If so, many UK insurers have something to worry about.
